articles.title: Lanterns: Could Hal Jordan Still Be Alive?
articles.summary: Don't count Hal Jordan out yet on Lanterns. Here's why the iconic Green Lantern might not be as dead as he seems...
articles.body:
Spoilers follow for Lanterns Episodes 1 through 6.

When Lanterns, the latest DC Universe show, debuted on HBO last month, it immediately hit many fans where it hurts with the revelation that Hal Jordan – the Green Lantern that so many of us grew up with – was being killed off . It was the first episode of his show, and there he was with a hole in his head, half frozen. What the heck!

Which isn’t to say that Kyle Chandler’s take on the character was a one and done. No, thanks to Lanterns being set across multiple time periods, we’ve been able to zero in on his relationship with his successor, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), in the 2016 era, plus we’ve seen some of the character’s earlier exploits as well, albeit briefly. But, of course, the 2026 time period features a dead Hal, including his funeral in Episode 6, “Bad Optics.”

But here’s the thing: Are we really sure Hal Jordan is dead? This is a superhero show, after all, albeit one gussied up like a rural crime thriller. We’ve still got two episodes left, and there are some clues that Hal maybe, just maybe, isn’t gone yet. Let’s take a look…

The Show Has Already Had a Bunch of Aliens Posing as Humans

Think about it: Everyone from Poorna Jagannathan’s Zoe Macon to Paul Ben-Victor’s Antaan to freaking Laura Linney’s character are aliens (or alien constructs) disguised as humans. And they’re just the examples who are played by noteworthy actors!

Usually we’ve only seen these extraterrestrials in their human forms, with the exception of Linney’s Lianna – who’s one of the Guardians of the Universe who created the Manhunters and the Green Lantern Corps, by the way – when she briefly shape-shifted into her true form earlier in the season.

The point is, Lanterns is full of characters walking around looking like and pretending to be something they are not. Is it so far-fetched to think that Hal’s dead body isn’t the real Hal? The last time we saw him alive was right after John punched him out in the diner, and Hal was clearly scared of something at that point, a state of mind we’ve never really seen him in on this show before. This worse- for-wear version of Hal pleaded with John to not reveal to anyone that his former mentee had been there, so there was obviously something going on that had Hal worried. Did he know he was about to face certain death, and he didn’t want John to be implicated in it? Or perhaps Hal knew there was some kind of bigger plan afoot that would involve the faking of his death, and he still didn’t want John to be connected to it?

The bottom line is someone like Hal, with his decades of experience and otherworldly connections, could surely figure out a way to fake his own death with a duplicate alien body if he wanted to. And speaking of friends in high places…

Hal’s Old Buddy Sinestro Just Broke Out of Space Jail

In this week’s episode, it’s confirmed the Green Lantern of 2026 is definitely not John Stewart, but rather Guy Gardner (Nathan Fillion), who visits John while he’s stuck in a jail cell in Rushville, Nebraska. During their not-at-all contentious chat, Guy reveals that Hal’s old mentor, and former Green Lantern himself, Sinestro (Ulrich Thomsen) has been broken out of “Spazkaban” – aka Space Azkaban (!)... basically the Guardians’ version of prison for the worst of the worst. And not just that, but Guy says that the first suspect for who might’ve helped Sinestro escape would’ve been Hal Jordan, if Hal didn’t have an alibi – namely being in jail himself on Earth. The only problem with that logic is it assumes that was the actual Hal who was in jail!

We first met Sinestro, albeit briefly, at the end of Episode 2 when Hal flew to space to talk with his old frenemy and try to pump him for information about the Manhunters. It was during that discussion – as we would later learn in Episode 4 – that Sinestro gave Hal some interesting advice, as he pointed out that John’s fearlessness would also mean he’d be “arrogant, overly confident, [and] thus blindly oblivious to your true intent.” It’s almost like Sinestro was giving Hal a roadmap as to how he could pull the wool over John’s eyes.

The obvious read here is that Hal took this advice and that’s what led to the disaster in Rushville in Episode 5 , but could it be that he was playing a much longer game? After all, the writers wouldn’t just tell us that Sinestro broke out of jail, only to then just drop that story thread, right? So whatever’s going on with that character, it would seem odd for it to not involve Hal…

There’s Something Fishy About Sheriff Kane’s Son Noah Macon…

So many secrets in this town! First there was the reveal that Kelly Macdonald’s Sheriff Kerry Kane had some kind of a dark past in Gotham City , and became – along with much of the town’s population – a member of Zoe Macon’s covert protection force as a means to escape that history. Zoe herself had the whole “I’m actually a Manhunter” thing going, and then there are all those aliens disguised as humans who we already talked about. But now, in the 2026 timeline, we also have to wonder what the truth is regarding Noah Macon (Shea Pritchard).

A high school football star that the whole town seems to be interested in, it’s obvious that the teen is a gifted athlete. He also seems to be a… great person, writing to FEMA over and over again until they repaired his school. (“He’s a natural-born leader,” his mom says.) And while Zoe wasn’t a biological relative as far as we know, she was his grandmother by marriage.

Let's also remember that enigmatic scene in Episode 5 where Zoe tells the young Noah (Cary Christopher) to remember what she taught him, just before everything goes to hell in Rushville. Is Noah some sort of failsafe or contingency plan for her?

The timing is certainly right for Zoe to have somehow created him when Kerry moved to Rushville. Is Noah also a Manhunter, if that’s the case? If this theory does pan out, I’m still not sure how it would connect to Hal faking his death… unless Hal has joined Kerry as a member of the Manhunter protection force (MPF?), and somehow this is all a ruse to draw out whatever Manhunter threat might still be out there.

You know, there’s one other possibility here, which is that, yes, Hal Jordan is in fact dead. But if we ever do get more Lanterns – we know a Season 2 is in the works, even if it hasn’t been officially greenlit yet – it could be that Kyle Chandler’s holographic version of Hal – his “Halogram” – would just be a way to keep the actor around, even if the actual Hal is dead and buried (in his suit but without his ring, of course).

The Halogram is one of the funnest aspects of the show, and he also represents a kinder, gentler version of Hal, which would give Chandler a different aspect of the character to play in a new season. Plus, he gets all the good lines…

DC Universe co-CEO James Gunn has hit back at criticism of HBO show Lanterns for apparently killing Hal Jordan “right away.”

The first episode of Lanterns showed a murdered Hal Jordan, played by Kyle Chandler, in 2026 before going back in time to 2016 to tell a seemingly unrelated story.

Showing the much-loved Hal Jordan with a hole in his head in the first episode of the show sparked a significant backlash from fans who had waited years for his live-action depiction in the DCU. Episode 6 doubled down on this by showing Hal’s funeral.

But there are question marks hanging over Hal’s death. Indeed, some aren’t convinced he’s dead at all. Following the conclusion of Episode 5, Lanterns has moved back to 2026 and switched into “whodunnit?” mode, with the central storyline revolving around John Stewart’s bid to solve the mystery of Hal’s murder. Some fans believe that over the course of the final two episodes, it will be revealed that the real Hal Jordan is alive and kicking, and the frozen corpse we saw in Episode 1 was a copy of some kind. (We recently explored the many ways Lanterns could explain that Hal is still alive .)

Still, some fans are very upset at Hal’s apparent death, and are sending angry messages to James Gunn on social media about it. Gunn actually responded to one person who had this to say:

“Maybe you should try and at least respect the characters that made the comics popular. Killing Hal off right away after we have waited 15 years to see him on screen again was the worst thing you could have done.”

Gunn clearly didn’t like that, and in his response dropped a clue that fans who think Hal is alive are on the right track.

“Hal's the star of TV series & he's in all the episodes so far,” Gunn began. “It's more live action screen time than all the live action screen time he's had combined throughout history. Kyle is amazing in the role. We more than respect him. We love him, despite his imperfections. Us knowing the time of his death, if that's exactly what that is, is absolutely not the same thing as killing him off right away. Hal is a big reason why the show is so popular with fans & non fans alike; sorry if you don't like it.”

DC Universe: Every Upcoming Movie and TV Show

Gunn’s position on this is clear: he feels like Hal’s had plenty of time on-screen over the course of the show, and it’s true he’s played a starring role in all the episodes so far. But it’s the line about his death that is being highlighted by fans:

“Us knowing the time of his death, if that's exactly what that is, is absolutely not the same thing as killing him off right away.”

“... if that’s exactly what that is,” is a line that, for some fans, pretty much confirms that there’s more to Hal’s death than it seems. Certainly, Chandler’s portrayal of Hal Jordan has gone down well with fans, who would love to see the character continue in the ongoing DCU. While there’s no suggestion he’s in next year’s Superman sequel, Man of Tomorrow, perhaps Gunn could see Chandler reprise the role in some other project, or maybe even a Lanterns Season 2.

Nathan Fillion’s Guy Gardner, however, is proving to be a throughline for the DCU. He’s in Superman, Peacemaker Season 2, Lanterns, and is expected in Man of Tomorrow.

articles.title: Heart of the Beast Review: Brad Pitt and His Combat Dog Go Ruffin' It in This Deeply Moving Wilderness Survival Drama
articles.summary: Heart of the Beast is a gripping wilderness survival film that will work especially well on dog lovers and those who like to see Brad Pitt get beaten up.
articles.body:
The lead actor in the new survival drama Heart of the Beast possesses rugged, movie star good looks, does almost all his own stunts, and delivers an understated, deeply moving performance. Brad Pitt is also in this movie. Pitt’s great here, too, but the titular heart of this gripping and emotional film is the dog, who is a very, very good boy indeed.

The movie even opens on the soulful face of Odin (real name Uber) , a former US Army combat dog who bears scars, has titanium in his mouth, and a prosthetic leg from injuries suffered in war. His handler/owner is James Belmont (Pitt), a now-retired Green Beret whose face we don’t clearly see until a few moments into the film. As much as James is the protagonist, the film is largely seen through the eyes of Odin.

James and Odin also both suffer from PTSD due to their combat experiences (yes, dogs get PTSD, too ). But they have each other, and the bond between them is stronger than steel, a mutual devotion and dependence that keeps them going after James’ plane crashes during a camping trip in the remote wilds of Alaska.

After suffering a heart attack while piloting his Cessna, James is put through the wringer as he and Odin (aka Odie) battle the elements, the terrain, and the wildlife over the next several days as they hike roughly 50 miles to reach the nearest road and get help.

Assuredly directed by David Ayer from a heartfelt screenplay by Cameron Alexander, Heart of the Beast throws nearly every survival scenario possible at James and Odin. From the unrelenting challenges of navigating the land to enduring gnarly injuries to storms to wolves and a grizzly bear, James and Odin encounter everything that could kill you in the woods except for a masked, machete-wielding serial killer.

I was emotionally invested in every moment of their brutal journey because of their relationship. There are as many “please don’t make me cry” moments in Heart of the Beast as there are “God, that looks excruciating” ones, with both James and Odin coming to each other’s aid to help them survive (although, in truth, the dog is pretty useless when it comes to setting up and breaking down campsites!).

Heart of the Beast isn’t as overtly emotionally manipulative as you might expect from a dog movie, simply letting Odin’s face and reactions do the work. But Brad Pitt also makes their whole dynamic work so well because of his deeply human performance. As tough and quiet as James is, his wounded soul and world-weariness are made clear just by Pitt’s eyes. That‘s some damn fine eye acting there, Brad Pitt, especially in the film’s closing moments.

And in a career that’s seen him get famously battered and bloodied in films like Fight Club, Snatch, Mr. and Mrs. Smith, Bullet Train, Fury, and even Meet Joe Black , to name a few, Brad Pitt gets the absolute shit kicked out of him for about three-quarters of Heart of the Beast’s run time. I can’t imagine just how physically grueling this shoot must have been for him.

Less effective are all the flashbacks to James and Odin’s combat experiences, not because they are poorly done but because they don’t convey much new information to the viewer. How both James and Odin ended up with their physical and psychological torments was made perfectly clear during a brief scene with a retired miner (J.K. Simmons) whom they encounter before the plane crash. The flashbacks could’ve been pared down, as they do tend to occasionally interrupt the flow. It’s a testament to how much I cared about James and Odin that I wanted the film to cut back to them and not leave me hanging.

Finally, on a technical level, I need to shout out the sumptuous landscape porn cinematography by Mauro Fiore and the haunting score by Jared Michael Fry. However, the CGI wolves and grizzly bear stick out like sore thumbs (although they’re nowhere near as bad as the CG dog in Call of the Wild ). I understand the practical reasons why they had to be used, but the attention they draw distracts from the otherwise very realistic look of the film.

articles.title: Handing Halo to Activision Makes Business Sense, but Is That Enough to Save the Series?
articles.summary: The next Halo game will be developed by Activision, but is the slick Call of Duty development pipeline enough to save Master Chief?
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Ryan McCaffrey, who worked at Official Xbox Magazine from 2002-2012 during the original Xbox and Xbox 360 era before joining IGN, where he remains “the Xbox guy” and has reviewed several Halo games, including the Master Chief Collection and Halo Infinite .

I’ll give Asha Sharma this: she is not afraid to shake things up. Whether you love or hate how she’s run the Xbox business in her first six months as CEO so far, there are no sacred cows with her. Whether it’s slashing Xbox Game Pass prices, nuking an unpopular marketing campaign, restoring console exclusives, telling Obsidian to make a damn Fallout game already , or signing Hideo Kojima after PlayStation cancelled Physint, she is more than willing to flip over some tables to try and get Xbox to a better place. Unfortunately, these decisions have also come paired with a lot of layoffs . To say the situation for all at Xbox is changing would be to put it very lightly.

When it comes to the very fundamentals of Xbox’s game DNA, though, Sharma’s latest power move is arguably her most earthshaking one yet. The next mainline Halo will be developed by Activision. Meanwhile, Halo Studios – the series’ custodians since 2011 – has been hit with significant layoffs.

Read that again. Halo Studios, once known as 343 Industries – the developer founded purely to create Halo games – will no longer be the creative drivers behind Halo. The keys to the Warthog have been taken away and given to Activision, makers of Call of Duty and the crown jewel of Microsoft’s $69 billion acquisition . The company had to crawl through regulatory broken glass in order to get approval for such a move, so I suppose this is one way to help further justify that kind of expense.

This doesn’t reflect well on Xbox’s handling of Halo over the past 15 years. You know you f*cked up pretty bad when the developer that was renamed to Halo Studios less than a year ago is now no longer making the next big Halo game. Like, holy shit. Let that sink in for a minute. But from where I sit, Halo Studios’ issues have never been with raw talent. I absolutely loved Halo 4’s campaign that centered on Master Chief and Cortana’s relationship, but its multiplayer failed to live up to the Halo standard. The opposite happened with Halo 5, whose awful campaign sat alongside a phenomenally good multiplayer. And Halo Infinite finally put two great halves together …for a minute, until the modern needs of maintaining a living multiplayer shooter couldn’t be met by the studio.

Instead, the problem has always seemingly been with management. From a reported reliance on an ever-cycling crop of contractors, to having to onboard every one of those said contractors with Halo’s proprietary Blam/Slipspace engine, it made the studio wildly inefficient. I’ve also personally heard from a well-placed source in the past week that leadership is “ineffective” and “makes me facepalm on a regular basis.”

But one source does not a complete narrative make. Let’s instead look at the results. We are already less than three months away from Halo Infinite’s fifth anniversary. And, based on the “reboot” of 343 Industries under the new Halo Studios name, its change of leadership, and shift from the proprietary Slipspace engine to Unreal Engine 5, the chances that the existing development structure could ship a new big Halo game in the next five years seems slim at best.

Sharma, who has already made it clear she wants Xbox to take a franchise-first approach to what it invests its resources into, must’ve come to the same conclusion. Giving the series to Activision says one thing above all else to me: she wants a Halo game soon. And Activision, whether you love it or hate it, does have a pretty sterling track record of getting big-budget blockbuster games done in a timely fashion. They’re not always great games (see last year’s Black Ops 7), but they’re usually at least pretty good, and they always ship on time. Has a Call of Duty ever missed a holiday ship date? Not that I can recall – that’s the power of multiple support studios working together.

So from that purely business perspective, handing Halo to Activision makes perfect sense. But what about creatively? That’s a more difficult question to answer. Activision undoubtedly has a ton of talent in-house, but Infinity Ward doesn’t seem like it’ll be escaping the Call of Duty salt mines anytime soon after successfully rebooting itself over its last few projects. Sledgehammer, meanwhile, has seemingly fallen out of favor following its tenure on some of Call of Duty’s weakest projects in recent years – Vanguard and Modern Warfare 3. But then again, Microsoft didn't say it was forming a new studio for Halo. It specifically used the term "purpose-built team." To me, that strongly suggests that a new team will be formed within an existing Activision studio that can plug directly into the established development pipeline. That leaves two likely candidates in my eyes: Treyarch and Raven.

Treyarch has arguably been Activision’s most dependable cash factory since it first created the Black Ops sub-franchise back in 2010. It was a success story born out of disaster, following Infinity Ward’s implosion and much of the studio’s founding team departing to form Respawn. Black Ops went on to become the flagship brand for many Call of Duty fans, particularly following the titan that was BLOPS 2. That winning streak came to a screeching halt last year, though, when Black Ops 7 released to middling reviews and disappointing sales . Perhaps that’s the signal that Treyarch needs a new focus. Interestingly, the studio recently said that it was “ ready to make something new ,” a quote which looks awfully suspicious given Sharma’s latest big move.

Putting Treyarch in charge of Halo would, in my opinion, be the safest move. Halo needs help, and Treyarch has been Activision’s most reliable studio that has a proven track record of elevating the world’s biggest franchise.

There’s another possibility, though: Raven Software. The pride of the Wisconsin game development scene has been stuck on Call of Duty for what feels like an eternity, but before that, its resume consisted of some absolute bangers. Heretic, Hexen, Quake 4, Star Trek Voyager: Elite Force, Star Wars Jedi Knight 2, Soldier of Fortune, and the 2009 Wolfenstein reboot are all examples of its FPS pedigree. Putting Raven in charge of Halo would be the bolder pick, if you ask me, and I’d be fired up if the studio got the call. And of course, it's also quite possible that this new team will pull talent from multiple Activision studios, but again, based on the way Microsoft worded it, I'd be willing to bet lunch that it's a new team within one of Activision's existing studios.

No matter who’s developing the next mainline Halo game, however, this move only makes me even more confident in a prediction I’ve been making for a while now on Podcast Unlocked: that the next major Halo game isn’t going to be Halo 7, or a sequel to Halo Infinite. It feels like far too much time has passed for a direct successor to make sense. Instead, I think what’s next is going to be a reboot.

A lot of Halo fans understandably hate the idea of the series starting afresh, but honestly, I think it’s time – especially now that the franchise is changing hands. By the time Activision is ready to roll, we’ll be 30 years deep, give or take, into the Halo canon. There are entire generations of players who missed out on some of Master Chief’s most important chapters. And considering Campaign Evolved was surely Halo’s first and last appearance on a PlayStation console, now that Sharma has made exclusives a priority again, a re-run of those formative years for a wider audience of players is no longer necessary. The reality is that it will be a new team picking up the mantle following a multi-year pause in Halo’s story, and that team is going to have its own ideas.

Campaign Evolved isn’t just a dead end when it comes to re-establishing the canon – it’s potentially also a technological loose end. Think about it: if one of the Call of Duty studios takes over, and Sharma wants Halo back on shelves as quickly as possible, you’d only slow that team down by having them pivot to Campaign Evolved’s Unreal Engine 5 when they’ve spent the past 15+ years working with Call of Duty’s proprietary tools. Those teams’ entire development pipelines are built around the bespoke IW engine and its unified toolset. And, for all the creative faults you could pick with Call of Duty, it’s hard to criticize them from a technical perspective. There’s almost zero chance that process gets messed with. Take all of that together and I just don’t see Activision picking up where Halo Studios left off in any way, be it narratively or otherwise.

So, can Activision save Halo? The cynical answer would be, “Well, they can’t do any worse.” But the real answer is: maybe. It depends on which studio and which team is entrusted with this billion-dollar task. Halo was the biggest first-person shooter series in the world before being dethroned by Call of Duty. How crazy is it that the very same people who defeated it are now being asked to resurrect it? If I’m being honest, though, as talented as Treyarch and Raven are, neither would be my first in-house pick at Xbox to revive Halo. I’d pick id Software (who might be done with Doom for now ) or MachineGames (who is reportedly busy with the conclusion to its Wolfenstein series). But both Treyarch and Raven are fully capable. Here’s hoping that whoever’s name is on the next Halo understands the assignment and is afforded every resource available to get it done properly.

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

Editor's note: this story has been updated to better reflect Microsoft's plans to have Halo developed by "a new, purpose-built team".

articles.title: CONFIRMED: Microsoft Hands Halo to Call of Duty Developer Activision as Part of Seismic Xbox Studios Shakeup
articles.summary: Microsoft has today confirmed that the next mainline Halo game will be developed by Call of Duty maker Activision, with mass layoffs hitting Halo Studios amid a significant restructure of its Xbox studios setup.
articles.body:
Microsoft has today confirmed that the next mainline Halo game will be developed by Call of Duty maker Activision, with mass layoffs hitting Halo Studios amid a significant restructure of its Xbox studios setup.

Xbox announced 268 layoffs today "across Halo Studios, other first-party studios, and the XGS management and central functions layer" as part of the ongoing cuts first announced in July . The layoffs, the majority of which are at Halo Studios, come as part of new Xbox boss Asha Sharma’s “reset” of Microsoft's gaming business that had already seen 1,600 staff lose their jobs in the summer. At the time, Microsoft said another 1,600 staff on top would also go this financial year.

"The actions completed since July, inclusive of the studio divestitures, bring us roughly three-quarters of the way through previously announced restructuring," Xbox Chief Content Officer Matt Booty said in a blog post . "I am deeply grateful for what our colleagues have built, and I know how difficult today will be for those leaving and the teams around them."

With Halo Studios gutted, Microsoft has handed Halo to Activision. Activision will develop "the next Halo title," Booty said, "led by a new, purpose-built team that is separate from ongoing development and plans for Call of Duty. A small team at Halo Studios will continue supporting the Halo community and games in-market."

Booty did not say when the next Halo game will come out, or if Activision plans to reboot the series or rotate it into its schedule of releases for Call of Duty, which hasn’t missed an annual release for 20 years.

Halo moving to Activision follows a string of tough releases for the franchise under Xbox's stewardship. Microsoft bought the Halo franchise when it purchased its original developer, Bungie, in 2000. Bungie then split from Microsoft to become independent again in 2007, and went to work on looter shooter Destiny as part of a high-profile, 10-year publishing deal with Activision. Meanwhile, Microsoft set up 343 Industries, so named after 343 Guilty Spark from the Halo games, to take Halo into a new era. 2012's Halo 4 was the first Halo game released by 343. It was followed by 2015's Halo 5: Guardians, which in turn was followed by 2021's much-delayed Halo Infinite. Halo Infinite in particular struggled, and this year's Halo: Campaign Evolved, a remake of the beloved first Halo game, suffered problems of its own.

In 2024, 343 Industries changed its name to Halo Studios and announced plans to work on multiple new Halo games that would all be developed on Epic's Unreal Engine. The announcements were unveiled in a seven-minute video shown ahead of the Halo World Championship's grand finals, which showcased the results of Project Foundry — an experimental project designed to show a Halo game built using Unreal Engine. While it was not much more than a tech demo, the video offered a glimpse at a fresh beginning for Xbox's flagship franchise in the wake of Halo Infinite's troubled launch. The question is, will any of that work be carried forward by Activision? Check out Ryan McCaffrey's reaction to today's Xbox news in his opinion article, Can Activision Save Halo?

Meanwhile, Xbox has moved Age of Empires developer World's Edge and Sea of Thieves developer Rare under the Activision umbrella, without confirming the legendary British studio's next game.

Rob Kostich, president of Activision issued the following statement:

"We’re thrilled to welcome Halo, Rare, and World’s Edge to Activision. It’s an honor and a responsibility that we do not take lightly. These teams and their games have inspired fans around the world for decades.

"For Halo, our goal is clear: make the greatest Halo game ever, worthy of its universe and legacy, while staying true to what made players love it in the first place. It is a bold ambition, one that this franchise deserves. We have already begun assembling a purpose-built team, unique in capability and talent, ready and excited to deliver this next chapter with the community.

"To the World’s Edge and Rare teams, we can’t wait to get to work together."

Every Video Game Franchise Xbox Owns After Acquiring Activision Blizzard

Outside Activision, Obsidian, developer of Grounded, The Outer Worlds, and Avowed, is now a Bethesda studio, as it begins work on a new Fallout game . Forza Motorsport developer Turn 10 is being merged with Forza Horizon and Fable developer Playground, and Candy Crush developer King now includes Microsoft Casual Games, which operates the likes of Solitaire, Mahjong, and Minesweeper.

Microsoft has also signalled its intention to close Hellblade developer Ninja Theory after two separate deals for a sale fell through . As per UK employment law, a consultation with staff has begun. Ninja Theory was working on the third entry in the Hellblade series, called Senua, but that game's future is in doubt .

There is no further news on the fate of Blade developer Arkane. Microsoft is currently negotiating with management over the future of the studio , following French employment law, so the process is further behind that of other Xbox studios. Booty said "consultation with Arkane remains underway and is expected to continue through the end of the year."

Psychonauts developer Double Fine and South of Midnight studio Compulsion had already managed to navigate their way to independence as part of the Xbox reset. Today, Booty confirmed that Undead Labs has now "successfully transitioned" on "similar terms" and, with a new publisher, will release State of Decay 3 day one on Game Pass.

"The goal is to strengthen our franchises and games by operating fewer business units, aligning groups that already work closely together, and focusing our publishing expertise," Booty added.

Today’s dramatic news sparks a number of unanswered questions: what does the future of Halo look like? What does Activision plan to do with Rare and Sea of Thieves? And where will the rest of the layoffs Microsoft announced were in the works in July come from?

The Xbox reset is the most significant restructure in the history of Microsoft's gaming business, and forms part of Sharma's drive to reach a billion people each day through video games by 2030. It follows continued poor financial results for Xbox and a collapsing profit margin, which Sharma has set about turning around by cutting costs and doubling down on big franchises such as Halo, Minecraft, and Fallout.

"Today, our focus should be on supporting those affected and treating one another with care and respect," Booty added. "I will spend time with our studios over the next week. At our October 6 town hall, we will come together as an ALL-XBOX team to reflect on our progress and look ahead to one of the strongest game lineups in our history."

Wesley is Director, News at IGN. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: The Beats 360 are what I’d bring to the gym if I hated earbuds
articles.summary: With swappable ear cushions and IPX4 water resistance, the Beats 360 should stand up better to sweat than other headphones from Sony, Bose, and Apple.
articles.body: Everyone has seen someone at the gym or running around their neighborhood wearing headphones that were never designed for workouts. Quite often those headphones are Beats. Good news for the earbud haters: The new Beats 360 over-ear headphones are durable and built to withstand sweat, with water resistance and swappable knit ear cups. And there aren’t many headphones out there like them. IP ratings are a bit out of the ordinary on any headphones, and the Beats 360 are the first IP-certified headphones from the company. Like Beats workout earbuds, the Powerbeats Pro 2 and Powerbeats Fit 2, the Beats 360 are rated IPX4, which protects against splashes of water and sweat. It’s the minimum rating I would recommend anyone use for a pair of workout headphones or earbuds if you want them to survive for more than a short time. There’s no way to avoid sweat accumulating around the ear cups when using headphones during a workout. But both wearables senior reviewer Victoria Song and I wore the Beats 360 while exercising, and we both found that the default performance knit ear cups on the Beats 360 did a good job wicking away that moisture. Still, by the end of her 40-minute run and my hour-long gym session, each of our headphones were wet and, as Victoria put it, “icky.” The ear cups are easily removable, so they can be cleaned separately — Beats recommends wiping them with a soapy solution, then a damp cloth with water only, and finally removing any leftover dampness with a dry cloth — and I didn’t run into any issues doing so. [Product: Beats 360 headphones | The Beats 360 have decent clamping force to keep the headphones secure during most workout movements without causing discomfort. For exercises where my head position was consistent — such as back squats, planks, and lunges — the Beats 360 stayed comfortably in place. Still, we both had moments where we needed to readjust them: sprints for Victoria and sit-ups for me. The movement isn’t excessive, and for explosive workouts — like the sprints, or even burpees — the Beats 360 would do in a pinch, but both of us still prefer earbuds. The Beats 360 come with performance knit ear pads, which are good for workouts (particularly because of the moisture wicking), but after a few hours of non-workout use, they make the side of my head itchy. But since it’s super easy and fast to change the ear cups, switching to one of the plush engineered leather options for regular listening is the right move (it’s the same material used with the Studio Pro headphones). [Image: [Image: The headphones come in black, white, light blue, and pink, and you can buy extra cushion sets to customize the look. The performance knit ear cups come in black, white, light blue, pink, navy, and a fluorescent green — though the plush are only in black and white. Each cushion kit comes with two ear cups and a headband and costs $50, although until the end of October, they’re available for $10 through Apple. There’s promo pricing for Canada, Australia, France, the UK, China, and Korea, as well. The Beats 360 have sensors that can tell whether you’re using the knit or plush ear cushions and automatically adjust the tuning. I didn’t hear any significant differences going back and forth between the two (although of course noise canceling was a bit better with the plush padding). The bass sounds nice and supportive, with good oomph for bass-heavy tracks without being too overpowering, like the Beats of old could be. And most of the high end sounds clear, if a bit peaky. My main issue is with the midrange, where it feels like a wash of sound. There isn’t much separation of guitars and vocals during the chorus of the Foo Fighters’ “The Pretender,” mostly because the shushiness of Taylor Hawkins’ cymbals overwhelm everything. It’s not a dealbreaker, but for $350, I prefer the Sony XM5. [Image: A quick twist locks the ear cup in place, with a tone played if the headphones are on. Noise-canceling performance is very good. Not as silent as the Bose Ultra Headphones Gen 2 or as solid a fit as the AirPods Pro 3, but the only reason I knew the gardeners were using their accursed leafblowers outside my window while I listened to some tunes on the Beats 360 was the lingering smell of gasoline. The ANC is enough to let you focus on your own music and block out the gym bro that says they know exactly how to correct your form. One of the benefits of all Beats headphones and earbuds is their integration across both Apple and Android ecosystems — an advantage of being owned by Apple, but not being Apple. On Apple devices, the Beats 360 support one-touch pairing, iCloud pairing, automatic switching between devices, audio sharing with AirPods and recent Beats headphones, Find My, and hands-free Siri. Native Android features include fast pairing, pairing across devices on the same Google account, audio switching (on supported Android devices), and Google’s version of Find My called Find Hub. Voice assistant works with Android, too, but requires a press of the play/pause button. It all makes them a great option for someone in either ecosystem. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Instead of a hard case, the Beats 360 have a soft-sided bag that has a magnetic clasp at the top and a loop on the back to hook to a clasp on your bag. I would have preferred a hard case at this price. They also have a replaceable battery, although there currently isn’t any documentation about the process or pricing for the replacement battery. For those who cannot abide earbuds or bone-conduction headphones at the gym, the options for solid, dependable headphones are few. The Beats 360, with their IPX4 rating and knit ear cups, are there for those who need something designed for that sweaty environment. And the replaceable ear cups and battery will help extend their life regardless. They’re not my first choice for everyday listening, but if I wanted to focus in on my reps without a worry — while showing off some color — I’d grab a pair.

articles.title: Activision is taking over Halo as part of a massive Xbox shake-up
articles.summary: The Xbox reset continues with major studio changes, layoffs, and more.
articles.body: Microsoft is announcing a massive restructuring of its Xbox studios today, months after laying off 1,600 Xbox employees and selling off studios. The latest changes will see Activision take on the Halo and Sea of Thieves franchises, as well as Age of Empires. Microsoft is also laying off around 268 Xbox employees as part of this restructuring, and likely closing Ninja Theory. Halo Studios will be significantly impacted by today’s changes and layoffs. The studio will continue to support existing titles like Halo Infinite and Halo: Campaign Evolved, but the next flagship installment in the Halo franchise will come from Activision instead. “Activision will also be developing the next Halo title, led by a new, purpose-built team that is separate from ongoing development and plans for Call of Duty,” says Xbox chief content officer Matt Booty in an internal memo. “A small team at Halo Studios will continue supporting the Halo community and games in-market.” That’s a significant change for the future of Halo, less than two years after Microsoft moved its Halo development to Unreal Engine 5. Halo Studios, formerly 343 Industries, has also undergone a leadership overhaul in recent years, as well as layoffs. “For Halo, our goal is clear: make the greatest Halo game ever, worthy of its universe and legacy, while staying true to what made players love it in the first place,” says Activision president Rob Kostich. “It is a bold ambition, one that this franchise deserves. We have already begun assembling a purpose-built team, unique in capability and talent, ready and excited to deliver this next chapter with the community.” World’s Edge, the studio behind the Age of Empires franchise, is joining Activision as part of this shake-up. Activision is also taking control of Sea of Thieves, with Rare’s UK team of developers joining the Activision side of Xbox. It’s not clear if there are any layoffs impacting Rare or World’s Edge as part of this shuffle. Former Rare studio chief Craig Duncan took on the role of head of Xbox Game Studios in 2024, and then resigned from Microsoft in June ahead of the big Xbox reset. Xbox Game Studios chief of staff Louise O’Connor also left the company alongside Duncan, after originally starting work at Rare in 1999. Microsoft is also officially acknowledging that Obsidian is moving over to Bethesda to work in close partnership on a new Fallout title. It’s not clear what kind of Fallout game will emerge, but with the success of the TV series I wouldn’t be surprised to see this particular title closely connected to the show. Turn 10 Studios and Playground Games are also merging into a single studio, focused on the future of Forza Horizon and Fable. Microsoft is also moving its casual games unit, responsible for Solitaire, Mahjong, and Minesweeper, from Bethesda to King. This is the second round of Xbox layoffs this year, but it might not be the last. Microsoft has already said that 3,200 roles are set to be impacted by Xbox cuts over the course of Microsoft’s 2027 financial year (which ends in June 2027). Today’s cuts bring the number up to nearly 1,900 in total, leaving more than 1,000 roles still yet to be announced. Microsoft now says it’s “roughly three-quarters of the way through previously announced restructuring.” Here’s the full memo from Matt Booty: > Team, > I’m writing to share several updates as part of the XBOX reset outlined earlier this year. > First, we are eliminating 268 roles across Halo Studios, other first-party studios, and the XGS management and central functions layer. The actions completed since July, inclusive of the studio divestitures, bring us roughly three-quarters of the way through previously announced restructuring. I am deeply grateful for what our colleagues have built, and I know how difficult today will be for those leaving and the teams around them. > Second, we are reorganizing our studios. The goal is to strengthen our franchises and games by operating fewer business units, aligning groups that already work closely together, and focusing our publishing expertise. > Activision will expand its remit to World’s Edge, as well as Rare. Activision will also be developing the next Halo title, led by a new, purpose-built team that is separate from ongoing development and plans for Call of Duty. A small team at Halo Studios will continue supporting the Halo community and games in-market. > Bethesda will expand its remit to include Obsidian, which will continue its current projects, including Grounded, as well as the new Fallout project made in collaboration with Bethesda Game Studios. > King will expand its remit to include Microsoft Casual Games, uniting our two global leaders in casual game design and live operations. > Playground and Turn 10 will come together as one studio focused on the Forza and Fable franchises. These two studios have been technological, creative, and franchise partners for over a decade, and today’s changes will formally move their work into one team. > Third, an update on our studio divestitures: In August, Compulsion and Double Fine returned to management with their IP, back catalogs, and runway funding. Undead Labs has now successfully transitioned on similar terms and, with a new publisher, will release State of Decay 3 day one on Game Pass. Unfortunately, two separate agreements for Ninja Theory fell through. We will now begin consultation with employees on a proposed closure while continuing to explore other paths forward. Consultation with Arkane remains underway and is expected to continue through the end of the year. > Today, our focus should be on supporting those affected and treating one another with care and respect. I will spend time with our studios over the next week. At our October 6 town hall, we will come together as an ALL-XBOX team to reflect on our progress and look ahead to one of the strongest game lineups in our history. > Matt

articles.title: Xbox is merging its Forza developers into a single studio
articles.summary: Playground Games and Turn 10 Studios staff will now focus on Forza Horizon and Fable together.
articles.body: Microsoft is uniting its two Forza developers into a single studio today, as part of a massive restructuring of Xbox. Playground Games, which develops Forza Horizon, and Turn 10 Studios, creators of Forza Motorsport, are merging together to focus on Forza Horizon and Fable. “Playground and Turn 10 will come together as one studio focused on the Forza and Fable franchises,” explains Xbox chief content officer Matt Booty in a memo. “These two studios have been technological, creative, and franchise partners for over a decade, and today’s changes will formally move their work into one team.” The closure of Turn 10 Studios leaves big unanswered questions around the future of Forza Motorsport, and whether Microsoft will ever return to the franchise or simply focus on Forza Horizon instead. More than 70 people at Forza Motorsport developer Turn 10 Studios were laid off last year, in a move that hit the vast majority of the studio. Over the past year, Turn 10 Studios has essentially been maintaining Forza Motorsport, and now those who remain will be moving over to Playground Games to work on Forza Horizon and Fable. The Playground Games and Turn 10 Studios changes are part of a larger reorganization of Xbox today. Activision is taking on the Halo franchise, alongside Sea of Thieves developers Rare and World’s Edge, the studio responsible for Age of Empires. You can read more about the latest Xbox shake-up right here.

articles.title: Microsoft Signals Intention to Close Down Ninja Theory After Deals to Save the Hellblade Developer Fall Through
articles.summary: Microsoft has signalled its intention to close down Hellblade developer Ninja Theory after two deals to save the Xbox studio fell through.
articles.body:
Microsoft has signalled its intention to close down Hellblade developer Ninja Theory after two deals to save the Xbox studio fell through.

In-line with UK employment law, a consultation with the staff at the Cambridge-based studio has begun. While Microsoft has said it is now working to close the studio, it remains open to an agreement to rescue the company.

"Unfortunately, two separate agreements for Ninja Theory fell through," Xbox Chief Content Officer Matt Booty said in a blog post issued today. "We will now begin consultation with employees on a proposed closure while continuing to explore other paths forward."

In June, at an Xbox Games Showcase event, Microsoft announced Senua, the third game in the Hellblade series. At the time, there was little concern about the game’s release. Indeed, there was little concern, publicly at least, about Ninja Theory itself.

But that all changed when optimism sparked by the positive showcase was shattered by new Xbox CEO Asha Sharma’s “reset” memo, which suggested mass layoffs and studio closures were to come. Confirmation came in July, when Ninja Theory was among the studios on the Xbox chopping block.

Amid the reports, fans expressed confusion at how Microsoft could announce Senua from Ninja Theory and then just days later tell the studio’s staff it planned to shut the company down. According to Game File , Microsoft allegedly planned to close or spin off Ninja Theory when it revealed Senua, and it did so thinking that “the promise of a newly announced game would help draw investor interest in the studio.”

Will Senua ever come out? IGN has yet to comment, but it’s looking increasingly unlikely unless a dramatic, 11th-hour deal can be struck that would save not just the studio, but the Hellblade franchise. Perhaps giving Ninja Theory hope is that Psychonauts developer Double Fine and South of Midnight developer Compulsion both navigated their way to independence and brought their intellectual property along with them, as well as funding for new games. Microsoft, it seems, is willing to part with IP to help get its studios out the door.

Ninja Theory’s Hellblade games have struggled commercially, and Microsoft is currently doubling down on its big franchises in a bid to raise revenue and profitability. It’s focusing on the likes of Minecraft, Halo (which is now under Activision’s umbrella), Fallout, and The Elder Scrolls as it looks to turn around the Xbox business over the next few years.

For more on all the big changes at Xbox announced today, check out our roundup .

articles.title: Adidas Officially Launches Limited-Edition Pokémon Collection
articles.body:
Adidas just dropped its limited-edition Pokémon collection , the latest in a pretty wild list of collaborations celebrating the franchise’s 30th anniversary.

The full collection includes over 10 new designs for a mix of the company’s most popular sneaker styles, including the Samba and Superstar II. Each shoe has an entirely distinct look inspired by a specific Pokémon, and the stars of the show aren’t too surprising.

Prices range from $60 to $180 with full family sizing. Even better? Every sneaker is available to buy right now.

Adidas Just Dropped Its 30th Anniversary Pokémon Collection

Some features, like the gold embroidered Pokémon x Adidas logo, appear across the collection, but each shoe generally stands on its own two feet (get it) as a unique release. Here’s the full list of what’s available in specific styles:

As you can tell, the collection includes a mix of full evolution lines (i.e. Charmander to Charizard) as well as some particularly iconic individual Pokémon like Pikachu and Mewtwo.

I got the chance to check out three specific shoes from the collection of time, and let’s just say I’m impressed. I don’t typically go for the most colorful looks in the world, but the designs have a range of boldness that lets you pick a vibe that goes best with your style. And, of course, based on whichever Pokémon you like best.

The Mewtwo Superstars are a soft purple with a sleek iridescent sheen. While every shoe includes a token-esque shoelace charm with its featured Pokémon’s face, this pair also comes with a funky “liquid” tag featuring the legendary’s classic Psystrike move. On the bolder side, the Charmander sneakers show a full graphic of the Pokémon blowing some literal Ember into the iconic Samba stripes.

It’s cool to see each shoe get its own little deep cut reference to a Pokémon’s type and even specific moveset. The (new!) illustrations of each Pokemon are all high quality, and the shoes themselves are, as you’d expect, pretty darn comfy.

As a limited-edition collection, it’s worth noting that stock may be limited. The Pokémon TCG side of things has been plagued by an ongoing scalping crisis that, these days, seems to extend to anything connected to the Nintendo franchise.

Speaking of, the collection forms part of some pretty extensive celebrations for Pokémon’s 30th anniversary. The beloved media powerhouse currently stands as the highest-grossing franchise of all time, and has already launched unique anniversary collaborations with Puma , Crocs , and even Krispy Kreme . I’m sure we’ll see plenty of more announcements through the end of the year, which, at the very least, will bring us slightly closer to the next mainline Pokemon generation .

articles.title: Sega Planned to Kill Sonic the Hedgehog Before Movie Success
articles.summary: Sega bosses were ready to ditch Sonic the Hedgehog before the franchise's hugely-successful live-action movie helped change their minds.
articles.body:
Sega bosses were ready to ditch Sonic the Hedgehog before the franchise's hugely-successful live-action movie helped change their minds.

That's according to Sonic Team leader and development veteran Takashi Iizuka, who has worked as a designer, director and producer on more than 30 games featuring Sega's mascot over the past three decades.

While the idea of Sega ditching Sonic seems shocking — akin to Pokémon abandoning Pikachu, or Mario shaving off his moustache — the Sonic series has certainly faced some tough years. Indeed, as Iizuka has now admitted, his tenure in charge of the blue blur included "good times" and also "the worst times."

Sonic the Hedgehog: All the Easter Eggs and Hidden References From the Movie

"It has been 35 years, which means it has been longer than actually my children, so I look upon this franchise like sort of like my own son," Iizuka told One More Game . "There had been good times, and there had been bad times... during the worst times, I was told by the higher-ups that we should cancel the entire franchise.

"I had to fight within the organization to keep the franchise as long as possible," Iizuka continued. "The biggest milestone for me was the first movie, that had been a great hit and definitely changed the course of this franchise."

Released in 2020, the first Sonic movie ended up earning a surprisingly solid $320 million and kickstarting a successful blockbuster franchise — though its success was far from assured. The series almost failed before it ever got started after the movie's first trailer was widely mocked for its "ugly" Sonic design, including horrible teeth. In a now-legendary move, Sega then decided to delay the movie to completely revise Sonic's design, ensuring it more closely matched the hedgehog's in-game appearance — and the rest is history.

Now, Sega has plans to continue pushing Sonic further beyond games, even if the hedgehog's foundation will remain on PC and consoles. Next year will see the launch of a fourth Sonic movie, a Netflix animation series is on the way, and Iizuka has said he expects "some sort of media almost every year from here on out."

"The franchise itself is rooted in video games," Iizuka concluded, confirming that Sega had no plans to ditch Sonic anymore. "We're just going to base everything upon the video games. That's our core principle."

What's next for Sega's Sonic game series? Iizuka says he has identified a desire from fans for more "more emphasis on story. So in coming years, I really want to create some game that has more emphasis on story." Iizuka also said he'd like to include more Shadow the Hedgehog, a character that he and an increasingly vocal group of fans both seem to enjoy. "If you have played Sonic Adventure 2, people may know that Shadow basically sort of died at the end of that game," Iizuka noted. "We were originally intending to just kind of 'die the character out' [kill him off'], but the character Shadow was just so very popular that we decided to revive him in Sonic Heroes."

In the meantime, Sonic the Hedgehog 4 launches in theaters on March 19, and the character is currently involved in a major crossover with Fortnite.

articles.title: Blizzard Reveals the World of Warcraft Forever Feature 'We Simply Must Hold the Line On'
articles.summary: Ever since Blizzard revealed World of Warcraft: Forever at Blizzcon 2026, the company has been laser-focused on maintaining its Classic+ identity, even if that means not implementing some quality-of-life features the game's retail version has had for years.
articles.body:
Ever since Blizzard revealed World of Warcraft: Forever at Blizzcon 2026 , the company has been laser-focused on maintaining its Classic+ identity, even if that means not implementing some quality-of-life features the game's retail version has had for years.

In a reply to GingiTV and Nobbel87 , two of the biggest WoW personalities on X/Twitter (albeit from complete opposite ends of the community), Blizzard developer Josh Greenfield confirmed that not implementing shared drops and tagging was "one of those things that we simply must hold the line on." He continued, saying "It’s hard to see the value in something like this when you are frustrated in the moment but it is extremely important to our social pillar to maintain some of this friction."

Yep, this. This is one of those things that we simply must hold the line on. I think there are other things we can do to help alleviate some frustration here but shared tagging is not it. It’s hard to see the value in something like this when you are frustrated in the moment but… — Josh Greenfield (@AggrendWoW) September 20, 2026

Yep, this. This is one of those things that we simply must hold the line on. I think there are other things we can do to help alleviate some frustration here but shared tagging is not it. It’s hard to see the value in something like this when you are frustrated in the moment but…

In the retail version of World of Warcraft, players who are questing or trying to farm rare spawns can all tag the same enemy (to a limit), so that everyone can get the rewards for killing it. This makes it a lot easier to play the game outside of a group, but it all but eliminates the need to group up with other players outside of high-end group content like dungeons and raids.

It's not hard to see why some people would want shared tagging implemented in Forever, too. The beta for this new version of old World of Warcraft has been incredibly popular , which means there's a lot of competition for anyone that just wants to kill some boars for some bones. The solution, which was suggested by Nobbel and confirmed by Greenfield is to "group up and get it done together," which will give people more opportunity to socialize, which is really what WoW Forever is designed for.

To Blizzard's credit, it seems like a huge portion of WoW Forever players agree with its approach. Most of the replies and quotes of Greenfield's post are along the lines of "The Classic team we trust 💙" from MrGMYT, and "shared tagging taught players to pay less attention to each other and soon became less social" from covingtown.

World of Warcraft: Forever is currently in Beta, which you can access by spending $60 on the Skyborne pack, but you'll only be able to play until level 20. The full game will launch on November 4, and will be included in your World of Warcraft subscription, just like any other version of Classic.

articles.title: Call of Duty's Activision to make next Halo game as Xbox cuts more jobs
articles.summary: The news comes as part of a "reset" announced by Xbox in July, with 3,600 planned job losses overall.
articles.body:
Xbox is cutting hundreds of jobs and making sweeping changes to the production of its flagship Halo franchise, as its company-wide "reset" continues.

Its latest reductions, forming part of a wave of ongoing layoffs, will impact staff at the studio which currently makes Halo - with Call of Duty publisher Activision to take on development of any future games.

Jez Corden of Windows Central said the change was a "dramatic move", while gaming analyst Christopher Dring said it raised questions over whether it could help revive what was once Xbox's "crown jewel".

It comes as questions also mount over the future of other notable Xbox studios, including Cambridge-based game developer Ninja Theory.

Xbox chief executive Asha Sharma said in July the Bafta-winning studio behind the Hellblade games would be spun off, alongside four others, amid its dramatic downsizing.

But Matt Booty, chief content officer at Xbox, wrote in a blog post on Tuesday that attempts to find a buyer for the studio had failed - with "two separate agreements" falling through.

He said Ninja Theory would now enter into consultation with employees on a proposed closure, though potential buyout talks are continuing.

Of the four other affected companies, three have now returned to management, while consultation for Arcane remains "under way", Booty added.

Xbox's announcement of a further 268 cut jobs comes after Sharma revealed in July that the company was "beginning the most significant restructure in Xbox history".

It saw 1,600 jobs cut immediately, amid 3,600 planned losses overall.

The company says it is three quarters of the way through its planned restructure.

Sharma said at the time that the Microsoft's gaming division had not been "healthy" and while platforms like its subscription plan Game Pass had "created meaningful value", they had not grown quickly enough.

In an interview with the BBC in August , she also pointed to the "crisis" in rising computing prices and hardware costs as another external pressure on the company.

Halo has been a hallmark of the Xbox brand since Microsoft's first entry into the console market in 2001, helping establish the firm as a major player in the industry.

Xbox said on Tuesday that Halo Studios, which recently released Halo: Campaign Evolved in July, would continue to support the game's community and work on existing games, as opposed to focusing on any new release.

Christopher Dring, editor-in-chief and co-founder of The Game Business, said the military sci-fi shooter was once Xbox's "crown jewel" but that hadn't been the case "for more than a decade".

"Halo was once to Xbox what Mario is to Nintendo," said Corden, "but years of mismanagement have eroded that".

Dring said bringing Halo under Activision's leadership "makes sense", though the company would be "mindful not to lose what makes Halo unique".

"For Halo, our goal is clear: make the greatest Halo game ever, worthy of its universe and legacy, while staying true to what made players love it in the first place" said Rob Kostich, Activision's president.

"We have already begun assembling a purpose-built team, unique in capability and talent, ready and excited to deliver this next chapter with the community."

As well as leading any new Halo game development, Xbox said Activision's remit would expand to manage the World's Edge studio, home to the Age of Empires franchise, as well as the studio Rare and its series Sea of Thieves.

The PlayStation rival also confirmed consolidations of some of its current companies - saying Elder Scroll-makers Bethesda would "expand its remit" to include Fallout New Vegas-makers Obsidian, and combining the studios behind Forza Horizon and Fable.

articles.title: Nodusfall Hands-On Preview: It’s Hoyoverse’s New One About Squadding Up and Killing Really, Really Big Monsters
articles.summary: I didn’t know anything about Nodusfall coming into it, but I came out very, very impressed by it. It’s no secret that the action game is in something of a bad way at the moment. Most things are kind of sauceless, a well-done steak. Nodusfall isn’t Devil Mary Cry or Ninja Gaiden or Bayonetta, but it feels great and has an impressive amount of things to manage for a co-op game.
articles.body:
It's a much darker art style and tone than we've been used to from Hoyoverse.

Nodusfall doesn't have Devil May Cry-type combat, but it does make you feel cool while in combat.

It's definitely not a soulslike (in a good way).

They told us that the Maldrake, the last of the three bosses my team squadded up against in Nodusfall, would be the one that would really try us. But it was the Qiongqi that really tested our group, wiping out our entire party the first time we attempted him. “Okay,” I said to our team. “Let’s do that again, but good this time.” Someone else pointed out that we hadn’t really been using our potions (I for the record, had, but I was just being judicious). We took a second to regroup and crack a couple more jokes, and then we ran back into the fight.

Nodusfall isn’t the kind of thing you’d expect from Hoyoverse. It’s not a bright game with an anime artstyle. It's a much darker, almost post-apocalyptic world where, according to Hoyoverse, “divine authority has crumbled and order has collapsed.” Sounds rough. You step into the role of a Weaver tasked with restoring order. The coolest thing about Nodusfall is that it’s drawing from mythologies around the world, combining and reimagining “universal motifs and classic narrative archetypes.” Almost every culture has a flood story; dragons are common in everything from Beowulf to Chinese myth. Combining those disparate elements from cultures across the world to create something new seems pretty natural.

In my experience with Nodusfall, that means squadding up with some folks and killing really, really big monsters. But first, I had to select a character. After fooling around with my options for a bit, I settled on a woman with a fire sword who believed the best defense was a good offense. As I landed hits, I would build up a bar I could cash in for stronger, fiery-er (that’s a thing, right?) heavy attacks. The rest of my squad saddled up with an archer, a magic user/healer, and a large man in armor with a massive greatsword who served as our tank.

Then we were out in the world, saddled up on our mounts (I chose a very handsome brown horse, though I recall there being several options). My demo was essentially a boss rush that culminated in the Maldrake, the one I told you about at the beginning that was supposed to test us. But we weren’t just teleported to a boss arena. There was a floating yellow trail for us to follow, of course, but there was also so much to see on the way there. Nodusfall is stunning. We passed a flowing stream, other travelers sharing the road. Animals roamed around us. Our demo was pretty directed, so I couldn’t go explore wherever I wanted, though I did get distracted by the world around me long enough to take a wrong turn, and had to turn my horse around to catch up to the rest of the group. But I couldn’t help but wonder how much exploring and interacting with the road would be part of the full release as we rode.

Eventually, our path ended at a waterfall, and we fought our first boss: the Cleaver Fellstone. He was the opening act, not challenging enough to really wipe us out but perfect for getting a taste of Nofusfall’s combat. Inevitably, someone will call Nodusfall a soulslike, and when they do, but I would politely disagree.

Yes, there are light attacks and heavy attacks and a stamina bar. But how systems function matters in a game like this, and Nodusfall has actual combos here, not just the same animations repeating ad nauseum. Can you dodge? Yes, but these things are speedy and they encourage you to take risks, not just sit back and wait your turn. In addition, you’ve also got three abilities and one ultimate, not just one or two abilities that you occasionally get to use now and then as a treat. Nodusfall feels like an action game (complimentary). Thank God.

The Cleaver was a big guy, but he was fairly slow, and while our team wasn’t great at coordinating yet – we were learning on the fly, you know – we were pretty good at figuring out our roles and doing our jobs individually. And just when it seemed like he was about to go down, in swooped the Qiongqi, a massive horned lion with wings straight out of Chinese myth, who did a good chunk of our work for us. We hacked away at the Qiongqi, but he retreated to his lair, and we followed. Here, in a brightly lit, massive cave, we attempted to finish what we started. And the Qiongqi kind of kicked our collective asses for a while.

Part of it was that he loved to take to the air, which meant my abilities were pretty useless. All of them were about closing horizontal distance or, like my ultimate, was a series of so many acrobatic slashes that it would make Cloud Strife blush, cashing out my charges for a sword lit up like a Zippo and bigger damage. I had to get my licks in when he came down to the ground. Otherwise, it was up to our archer to lay on the pain. Our battle took on an interesting flow: myself and our tank up close when we could be, our healer/magic user in the middle to keep us all topped off, and our archer hanging back and shooting.

What really got us into a “Let’s do that again, but good this time” situation were these nasty red orbs that he summons, which damage you over time if you don’t take care of them. Since my beautifully animated, highly damaging abilities – which I always loved to see come off cooldown; Nodusfall feels like an action game, but like basically every modern video game, it wants to ensure that you’re never having too much fun – were useless while the Qiongqi was in the air, I decided to make the orbs my priority.

But the space was big, and even sprinting full speed, it took me a while to get to them, and they do a lot of damage real quick if you don’t. Down goes Frazier, and by Frazier I mean “all of us.” After regrouping (and a few of us realizing they had potions) and taking a second to work on our strategy, we tried again. A few of us went down during the fight, but we could pick each other up and get back into the fight if we were on the ball, and if we weren’t, we spawned right outside the fight and could run in. The Qiongqi tested us, but we came out of it stronger for it, and in the end, he fell to an absurdly cool execution animation involving all of us when we staggered him for the final time that involved a ghostly giant with an axe bringing said axe down on the Qiongqi’s neck.

Then it was time for the Maldrake, who came complete with a rider that had me saying, “Yo, why is there a Nazgul here?” out loud. This fight was trickier because, well… dragon. He could fly, breathe fire, swipe you with his tail, the whole nine yards. And his ride was no slouch, either. He was definitely doing his best Artorias the Abysswalker impression visually, but his attacks were wide and sweeping.

By that time, though, I was fully in tune with my character, dancing under the dragon’s tail, dodging through the knight’s blows, building up my fiery heavy attacks and unleashing my abilities and ultimates when I had them. Nodusfall isn’t Devil May Cry; it just doesn’t have the technical depth, but I always felt cool while I was playing it, which goes a long way, and working with my team was fun. After we did enough damage, the knight dismounted to meet us on the field himself while the dragon attacked from the air. Then, our tank transformed into a giant himself, and we watched the two of them go at it. Pretty rad.

Just when I thought the fight was over and we’d brought the knight down, he leapt into the air, stabbed the dragon in the chest, and stole the dragon’s remaining life. Props for style, admittedly, but now he was alone, and while he definitely seemed stronger, we knew the drill and hit him with everything he had. Eventually, my ultimate took him down, and the development team, who had been watching behind us, cheered as they had for every other squad. We’d been the last to finish, but it hadn’t been by much, and given how long the Qiongqi had taken us, I felt pretty proud of how we’d come together for the final battle. When Nodusfall scored our individual performances at the end, I was happy to learn I’d done the most damage. Fire swords forever.

I didn’t know anything about Nodusfall coming into it, but I came out very, very impressed by it. It’s no secret that the action game is in something of a bad way at the moment. Most things are kind of sauceless, a well-done steak. Nodusfall isn’t Devil Mary Cry or Ninja Gaiden or Bayonetta, but it feels great and has an impressive amount of things to manage for a co-op game. It was one of the best games I played at Gamescom, and I’m really eager to see what other mythical beasties Hoyoverse is cooking up for me to whack with my fire sword. Everybody’s got a type.

articles.title: Rayman Legends Retold Does a Good Job of Scratching That Platforming Itch | IGN Preview
articles.summary: Rayman Legends Retold isn't breaking any new ground – not visually and not gameplay-wise, not that it should be expected to since it's a remake, after all – but it is a clean remake chock-full of content both new and old at a pretty nice value. It might be of particular interest to the Switch 2 crowd that isn’t getting the GTA 6 meteor landing in their lives this Fall (particularly in light of a new 3D Mario platformer’s continued absence and Super Mario Bros. Wonder being a couple years old now), and/or to the younger crowd that hasn’t played the series before. Here’s hoping it leads to a brand-new Rayman adventure sooner rather than later.
articles.body:
The remake looks good, but not necessarily better than the 2D original it updates.

It's got new content to add on to what's already here, along with an entire other Rayman game bundled with it.

It still plays really well as a pure platformer.

I’m going to get my most subjective opinion out of the way here first, before I tell you about my experience actually playing Rayman Legends Retold, the just-delayed remake of 2013’s absolutely stellar 2D platformer. Here goes: despite being 13 years newer, I don’t think this 2.5D remake looks any better than the gorgeous 2D original…which seems like something that, if you ask me, shouldn’t be up for debate if you’re going to remake a game. And as such, I’m not sure how necessary this remake is. Our own Michael Higham arrived at the same opinion after he did our first preview .

But that’s not to speak ill of what is being presented in Rayman Legends Retold. It looks good , to be explicitly clear, regardless of whether or not you’ve ever seen the 2D original, and even better, it still plays fantastically well. This is a platformer that has aged quite well in the gameplay department – at least, based on the three hours I played of Retold recently, combined with the fact that I hadn’t touched Legends since it originally released one Grand Theft Auto ago.

That being said, based on what I’ve played so far, it does nicely integrate some new content with the old. It’s got new musical levels, where you’re essentially platforming to the beat of a song (I played the “Macarena” stage). It’s also got new stages and a revamped Kung Foot mode. Heck, Ubisoft is even throwing in the entirety of Rayman Origins: Enhanced Edition as a sweetener with the standard, $40 version of Retold.

If you’ve played a Rayman platformer before then you’ve probably read all you need to at this point, but if you’re new to the series, Rayman Legends Retold is a pure side-scrolling (mostly) platformer where, not unlike in Mario’s 2D platforming adventures, you can absorb at most one hit (read: any contact whatsoever) from an enemy before dying and resetting to the most recent checkpoint. Although I should note that Rayman Legends Retold does its very best to avoid frustration, as there are optional “golden hearts” you can pick up; they appear when you respawn after dying a few times in a row at the same point. And if the game still detects you banging your head against the proverbial wall, you have the option to invoke the “Fairy Blessing” that puts our limbless hero in a protective bubble and lets you literally float right by whatever challenge you’re currently frustrated with.

Each hub area, meanwhile, has a unique theme, and the variety was both impressive and appreciated. I started my hands-on in a food-themed zone called “Spoiled Rotten” where I was jumping off giant cucumbers and tomatoes and occasionally being shrunk down to the size of an ant through carefully placed trumpets that let me navigate the innards of a watermelon, as one example. The “What the Duck” stage here was marked by everything being made of sweets and pastries, and here I had a hungry flying helper named Murphy who would zip around in specific patterns near certain bits of culinary geometry, leaving me to press LB or Y to have him eat through whatever he passed through. These were often enjoyable platforming challenges unto themselves, as I had to figure out how to navigate my way through the freshly eaten spots unscathed before the cakey walls regenerated a few moments later.

I played one boss fight in a completely different world against a giant Luchadore, too, which mixed things up with timed attacks and big, bold setpieces. Pretty standard platforming fare, but really well-executed. And I suppose that’s where I landed after my few hours with Rayman Legends Retold. It’s not breaking any new ground – not visually and not gameplay-wise, not that it should be expected to since it's a remake, after all – but it is a clean remake chock-full of content both new and old at a pretty nice value. It might be of particular interest to the Switch 2 crowd that isn’t getting the GTA 6 meteor landing in their lives this Fall (particularly in light of a new 3D Mario platformer’s continued absence and Super Mario Bros. Wonder being a couple years old now), and/or to the younger crowd that hasn’t played the series before. Here’s hoping it leads to a brand-new Rayman adventure sooner rather than later.
